questions.q: Why can a page on another site make Ada's browser send a transfer request that the wallet accepts?
questions.explain: This is ambient authority: the credential travels with the request automatically. The other site never sees the cookie and never reads the answer; it only needs the request to be sent.
options: The other page can read Ada's session cookie with document.cookie
The browser attaches the wallet's cookies to every request to the wallet, whoever started it
The same-origin policy allows other sites to read the wallet's responses
Form submissions skip the server's authentication

questions.q: The session cookie is HttpOnly. What does that do against CSRF?
questions.explain: HttpOnly protects the cookie's value from page JavaScript (useful against XSS). CSRF does not need the value, only that the browser sends it. SameSite is the cookie attribute that controls sending.
options: It stops the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests
Nothing: it stops scripts from reading the cookie, not the browser from sending it
It forces the request to use HTTPS

questions.q: A session cookie has SameSite=Lax. On which request started by another site does the browser still send it?
questions.explain: Lax sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations so links from email still arrive logged in. That is why a GET handler must never change data.
options: A hidden form that POSTs to your transfer route
A normal link the user clicks, which opens your page with GET

questions.q: Which cookie is the best fit for SameSite=Strict?
questions.explain: Strict is never sent on requests from other sites, not even link clicks. That is the safest choice for high-value actions, at the cost of users following a link arriving without that cookie.
options: A cookie that authorises admin actions or money moves, where arriving logged out from a link is acceptable
A cookie for a widget embedded in other people's sites
Every cookie, because Strict is always best
A cookie that must be read by page JavaScript

questions.q: Why is SameSite not enough on its own?
questions.explain: A request from blog.wallet.example is same-site for app.wallet.example. If a subdomain runs untrusted code or can be taken over, SameSite does not help. Add a token or an origin check as a second layer.
options: Browsers only apply it to GET requests
Every subdomain of your registrable domain counts as the same site, and old browsers ignore the attribute
It only works over HTTP, not HTTPS
Attackers can remove it from the cookie

questions.q: Why does a CSRF token in a hidden form field stop the forged request?
questions.explain: The same-origin policy stops the other site from reading your form page. Without the per-session secret, the forged request fails the server's token check.
options: The token is encrypted, so the other site cannot change it
Browsers refuse to submit forms that contain hidden fields
The other site cannot read your pages, so it cannot learn the token the request must carry
The token makes the request a preflighted CORS request

questions.q: A server issues one CSRF token per session but accepts any token it has ever issued. What can an attacker do?
questions.explain: A token proves something only if it is checked against this session. Otherwise the attacker's own token works in the victim's request.
options: Nothing, the token is still secret
Log in with their own account, take their own valid token, and put it in the forged form

questions.q: What makes Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site useful for CSRF checks?
questions.explain: They are controlled by the browser. A request with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or a foreign Origin can be refused before the body is read. A non-browser client can send anything, but it also does not hold the victim's cookie.
options: They are signed by the server
The browser sets them, and page JavaScript cannot set or change them
They are only sent by trusted clients

questions.q: An API authenticates with Authorization: Bearer …, added by the app's own JavaScript. No cookies are used. Does it need CSRF tokens?
questions.explain: CSRF relies on credentials the browser adds automatically. A bearer token added by your own script is not sent by requests other sites start. The risk returns if the token moves into a cookie.
options: Yes, every API needs CSRF tokens
No: another site cannot make the browser add that header, so there is no ambient credential to abuse

questions.q: The wallet test sends a request with the correct Origin but no token. Why test that, if the origin check already blocks real attacks?
questions.explain: With one test for the whole attack, a refactor could delete a whole layer and the test would still pass thanks to the other layer. One test per layer keeps every layer honest.
options: To check the origin header is parsed
To prove the token layer works on its own, so removing one layer by accident makes a test fail
Because browsers sometimes send the wrong origin

questions.q: A server copies the request's Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What does this allow?
questions.explain: The browser's rule is "exact origin plus credentials true". Reflection satisfies it for every origin, so every site can read the user's data, and a token read from a response defeats the CSRF token too.
options: Nothing, because browsers reject reflected origins
Only same-site pages to read responses
Any website to read the logged-in user's responses, including any CSRF token they contain
Any website to send requests, but not read them

questions.q: Why should a server add Vary: Origin when its CORS headers depend on the origin?
questions.explain: Vary tells caches which request headers change the response. Without it, a cache could store the answer for a trusted origin and replay it for a different one.
options: Browsers ignore CORS headers without it
So a shared cache never serves one origin's response, with its permission header, to another origin
It is required for cookies to be sent

questions.q: Which statement about CORS is true?
questions.explain: CORS is a browser rule for reading. Simple requests (like form posts) are still sent, and non-browser clients ignore CORS completely.
options: CORS stops curl from calling your API
CORS stops other sites from sending requests to your API
CORS only tells browsers which other origins may read responses; authentication and permissions protect the data
CORS replaces the need for CSRF protection

questions.q: Why should an allow-list never contain the origin null?
questions.explain: The null origin does not identify anyone. Any page can create a sandboxed frame whose requests carry Origin: null.
options: Sandboxed frames and local files send it, so an attacker can produce it on purpose

questions.q: A search page puts the q query parameter into its HTML without encoding. Which kind of XSS is that?
questions.explain: The data comes from the current request and goes straight back in the server's HTML, so whoever controls the link decides the markup. Stored XSS comes from saved data; DOM XSS happens in page JavaScript.

questions.q: The server sends a static page. Its script does el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1). Which kind of XSS is this, and where is it fixed?
questions.explain: The fragment is never even sent to the server. The page's own code moves a source (the URL) into a markup sink, so the fix is in that code.
options: Reflected; fix it on the server
Stored; fix it in the database
DOM-based; fix it in the page's JavaScript, for example with textContent
It is not XSS because the server never sees the hash

questions.q: Why does an XSS bug defeat CSRF tokens and CORS?
questions.explain: The same-origin policy protects the attacker's script once it runs inside your origin. That is why output encoding and CSP matter so much.
options: The attacker's script runs in your origin, so it can read your pages (and their tokens) and send same-origin requests
XSS changes the server's CORS configuration
It does not; CSRF tokens stop XSS

questions.q: A profile shows <a href="${website}">. The value is HTML-escaped. What is still missing?
questions.explain: Escaping stops the value from leaving the attribute, but javascript:… contains no characters to escape and still runs when clicked. URL contexts need a scheme check.
options: A scheme allow-list: parse it with URL and accept only https: or http:
Wrapping it in encodeURIComponent and nothing else

questions.q: Product descriptions come from a rich-text editor and must keep bold text, lists and links. What should the server do?
questions.explain: Escaping would show the markup as text. Hand-written regex filters miss event attributes, odd nesting and parser quirks. A sanitizer parses the HTML and keeps only what the allow-list names.
options: HTML-escape them like any other text
Remove <script> tags with a regular expression
Run them through a maintained HTML sanitizer with an allow-list of tags and attributes

questions.q: What is the role of a Content-Security-Policy against XSS?
questions.explain: Encoding is the fix; CSP limits the damage of the encoding bug you have not found yet.
options: A second layer: when an encoding bug slips through, the browser refuses to run the injected script
It stops other sites from sending requests to you

questions.q: Which of these nonce setups protects the page?
questions.explain: The attacker must not be able to predict the nonce of the page the victim will load. A fixed or guessable nonce can simply be copied into the injected tag. 'unsafe-inline' would allow inline scripts anyway.
options: A long nonce stored in configuration and reused for every response
A fresh random nonce per response, the same in the header and in the page's own script tags
A nonce derived from the user id
A nonce in the header only, with 'unsafe-inline' as a fallback

questions.q: What can a CSP in a <meta> tag not do that the header can?
questions.explain: Browsers ignore frame-ancestors, report-uri and sandbox in meta policies. Send the policy as a header.

questions.q: You are adding a strict CSP to an old app with many inline scripts. What is the safe rollout?
questions.explain: Report-Only makes the browser report violations without blocking, so you find your own inline scripts before users see broken pages.
options: Send Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first, fix what it reports, then enforce
Enforce immediately and fix whatever breaks
Put the policy in a meta tag so it is weaker

questions.q: Which header stops the browser from treating an uploaded .txt file as HTML or script?
questions.explain: nosniff makes the browser trust the declared Content-Type instead of guessing from the content.

questions.q: What does naming the session cookie __Host-sid add?
questions.explain: The prefix is enforced by the browser. It locks the cookie to exactly your host, which blocks cookie injection from other subdomains.
options: The browser accepts it only with Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, so sibling subdomains cannot set or overwrite it
It sends the cookie to all subdomains

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: endsWith only looks at the last letters. myshop.example ends the same way, and the scheme is never checked. An exact Set lookup accepts only the listed origin.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without ^ and $, the pattern matches anywhere inside the string, so a longer domain that starts with yours passes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The trailing comma produces an empty string, which becomes an allowed "origin". Trim and filter empty entries when you read the list from configuration.
questions.code:
const trusted = new Set("https://shop.example,".split(","));
console.log(trusted.size, trusted.has(""), trusted.has("https://shop.example"));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A single replace with one regular expression visits each character once, so the & in a new entity is never escaped again. All five special characters are replaced.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A plain template string pastes the text in as it is, so the tag is in the HTML: the browser would build an <i> element. That is stored XSS in its smallest form.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify leaves </script> inside the string, and the HTML parser would end the script there. Replacing < with \u003c leaves only the real closing tag, and the JSON still reads back the same.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: URL normalises the address (adding the /) and lower-cases the scheme, even with a leading space and capitals, so the check sees javascript: and refuses it. A relative path throws without a base, so it is refused too.

questions.q: A developer checks URLs with startsWith("http"). What does this print?
questions.explain: A prefix test is not a scheme check: httpx:alert passes although it is not HTTP at all. Parse with URL and compare protocol exactly.
questions.code:
const check = (value) => value.startsWith("http");
console.log(check("https://ada.example"), check("httpx:alert"), check("JavaScript:void(0)"));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: timingSafeEqual throws on different lengths, so the length is checked first. The x.length > 0 check makes a missing token on both sides fail instead of "matching".
options: true, then an error is thrown

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A foreign origin and a cross-site fetch are refused. A request with neither header (curl, a server) passes this layer, because it cannot carry the victim's browser cookie; the token check still applies to it.

questions.q: This function models the browser's SameSite rule. What does it print?
questions.explain: A cross-site form POST gets no Lax cookie, which is what stops classic CSRF. A cross-site link (GET, top level) still carries it. Strict sends it only when the request starts on your own site.

questions.q: Write isTrustedOrigin(origin) for the allow-list setting below. Trim spaces, ignore empty entries, and accept only exact matches. The program should print true false false false.
questions.explain: Build the Set once from configuration. Without the trim, " https://mobile.wallet.example " would never match; without the filter, the trailing comma would allow the empty origin.

questions.q: Finish corsHeaders(origin). It must always include Vary: Origin, and add Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the origin itself) and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: "true" only for trusted origins.
questions.explain: Unknown origins get no permission at all, so the browser hides the response from them. Vary goes on every response, because the answer depends on the origin either way.

questions.q: Write escapeHtml(value) that replaces &, <, >, " and ' with &, <, >, " and ', and converts non-strings with String.
questions.explain: One pass with a character class escapes each character exactly once. With a chain of replaceAll calls, & must come first, or the entities you just created would be escaped again.

questions.q: Write a tagged template html that HTML-escapes every interpolated value (use the given escapeHtml) and returns a string. The program should print the list item with the review text escaped.
questions.explain: A tag function receives the fixed parts (strings, written by you) and the values separately. Escaping only the values keeps your markup and turns the user's into text. That is how auto-escaping template engines work.

questions.q: Write safeHref(value): return the normalised URL (url.href) if it parses as an absolute URL with the https: scheme, otherwise null. Do not use startsWith.
questions.explain: Parsing gives you the scheme the browser will use. new URL throws for text that is not an absolute URL, so the catch turns it into null.

questions.q: Write stateScript(state) that returns <script>window.STATE = …</script> with the state as JSON, escaped so that no < from the data appears in the output. The program checks there is exactly one closing tag and that the JSON reads back unchanged.
questions.explain: In the output string, "\\u003c" is the six characters \u003c, which JSON reads back as <. The HTML parser, which runs first, never sees a closing tag inside the data.

questions.q: Write buildCsp(nonce) that returns the strict policy from the lesson: script-src with the nonce and 'strict-dynamic', then object-src 'none', base-uri 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none', joined with "; ".
questions.explain: Building the policy from a list keeps each directive readable in review. In the server, the nonce comes from randomBytes(16) on every response, and the same value goes into your own script tags.

questions.q: Write allowRequest({ method, origin }) for a cookie-authenticated app at https://wallet.example: GET and HEAD are always allowed (they must not change data); any other method is allowed only when origin is missing or equals the app origin.
questions.explain: Safe methods pass because they must never change state. A missing Origin means a non-browser client, which does not carry the victim's cookie; the CSRF token check still runs for it later.
